A Week Inside My TikTok Feed: What My Own Data Said About How I Scroll

Why I tracked my own scrolling

For one stretch of time I treated my own TikTok feed like a dataset. After every session I filled out a short form – the date, the time of day, roughly how many videos I had just watched, the kind of content that dominated the feed, and how many sponsored posts I had been served. By the end I had 44 sessions logged, and a question I wasn’t sure I wanted answered: what does my scrolling actually look like from the outside?

The four charts below are my attempt to find out.

📱 How many TikToks did I watch each day?

Lollipop chart showing the total number of TikTok videos I watched on each logged day across the observation period. Each day appears as a light grey vertical stick rising from zero, topped with a dark grey point. Days where no session was logged appear as blank space along the x-axis, so the gap in data collection between Project 2 and Project 4 is visible rather than hidden by a connecting line.

The first thing I wanted to see was the shape of my scrolling over time. One honest caveat up front: there’s a gap in the middle of the chart. I only started logging sessions when I was asked to for class (first in Project 2, and again now in Project 4), so the blank stretch in between isn’t quiet days – it’s days I wasn’t recording at all. That’s why I switched this chart to a lollipop instead of a connected line: each stick is one day’s actual data, and the gaps are honest gaps.

What remains is still telling. Across the days I did log, I racked up roughly 1516 videos – an average of about 34.5 per session. The tallest sticks tend to line up with the evenings I told myself I’d “just check TikTok for a minute,” which, looking at this chart, was almost never true.

When does each kind of content dominate my feed?

Grouped bar chart of the average number of TikTok videos watched per session, split across four times of day (Morning, Afternoon, Evening, Late Night). Bars are coloured by main content category, so each cluster shows which kinds of content drove the longest sessions at that time of day.

The feed isn’t the same all day. Different kinds of content dominate different time slots, and the bars make that obvious in a way my memory never could. Across the whole week, my most-shown category was Comedy – which says as much about the algorithm as it does about me. The bigger surprise was how cleanly the day splits into “casual scrolling” hours and “I’m not putting this phone down” hours.

The mornings I thought were quick check-ins were rarely quick.

More scrolling = more ads?

Scatter plot of the number of sponsored posts seen against the number of videos watched per session. Each point is one session, coloured by main content category and shaped by whether the category is entertainment-style (Comedy, Music, Gaming, LifeStyle) or not.

There’s a price for staying on the app, and you can see it: the more videos I watched, the more ads I was served. But the relationship isn’t perfectly linear - some categories load me up with sponsored posts much faster than others. Over the whole observation period I was shown 350 sponsored posts, roughly 8 per session.

What jumps out from the scatter is that the ad-load isn’t random – it tracks the kind of content. The category that served me the most sponsored content per video watched was LifeStyle, at roughly 26.6% of videos being ads. That makes sense: product-led niches (think beauty reviews, tech unboxings, food brand tie-ins) are essentially built around sponsorship – creators in those spaces are the ad. Compare that to Gaming, where my feed felt almost ad-free by comparison. The same scroll buys very different amounts of selling depending on what I’m scrolling through.

Does longer scrolling actually make me feel worse?

Boxplot showing the distribution of mood-after-session ratings (1 = very bad, 5 = very good) across three binned session lengths: Short (under 10 minutes), Medium (10–30 minutes), and Long (over 30 minutes). Each box shows the median, interquartile range, and outliers of mood ratings within that session-length bucket, so any shift in mood as sessions get longer is visible at a glance.

This is the chart that justified the two new questions I added for this project. The whole reason I asked myself how long each session was and how I felt afterwards was to find out whether staying on the app longer actually cost me something I could measure. Across all my logged sessions, my average mood-after-session sat at about 3.73 on a 1–5 scale – squarely in “neither great nor terrible” territory.

The more telling pattern isn’t the median, it’s the spread. My Medium sessions (10–30 minutes) had a median mood of 3 with a fairly tight box around it. My Long sessions (30+ minutes) had the same median of 4, but a noticeably wider box reaching up toward 4 and a whisker stretching to 5. In other words: longer scrolls aren’t reliably better or worse on average – they’re just less predictable. Some leave me fine, some leave me drained, and that variance itself is the part I’d want to fix. I haven’t logged any sessions under 10 minutes yet – apparently that’s not really how I open TikTok.

What I learnt

Watching my own data plotted out is more uncomfortable than I expected it to be. The peaks on the daily chart line up with the days I remember feeling drained. The category bars match the moods I was in. The ad scatter shows me, very plainly, that the longer I stayed, the more I was being sold to.

I’m not sure I’ll quit. But I can’t pretend I don’t see it anymore.
